## A. Rationale

Intracortical brain-computer interfaces let people with paralysis control
computers and communication devices directly from neural activity. Their central
unsolved engineering problem is not accuracy on day one — it is **reliability
over months**. The recorded signal is not stationary: electrode impedance
changes, individual units are lost, and the relationship between neural activity
and intended movement drifts. Longitudinal hardware studies establish the
timescale and the smoothness of this process — Sponheim et al. (2021) across
>6,000 datasets and nine years, Hughes et al. (2021) across five years in a human
participant, and Barrese et al. (2013) on failure modes across 78 arrays.

The field's response has been almost entirely **corrective**: realign the latent
dynamics (Karpowicz et al., 2025), adversarially match distributions across
neuron turnover (Ma et al., 2023), impute degraded channels (Kuo et al., 2025),
or recalibrate on a schedule. Each of these treats drift as a nuisance to be
removed. Pun et al. (2024) came closest to treating it as information, showing
that a KL-divergence measure of neural instability tracks closed-loop
performance — but, as their own framing makes clear, that is a **nowcast**: it
estimates present performance from present neural activity. It does not ask
whether the signal anticipates a decline before the decline occurs.

That gap matters practically. Recalibration is not free: it costs the user time,
requires supervised data, and on many systems interrupts use entirely. A system
that recalibrated only when it was about to need to would give back that time. A
system that warned before failure, rather than after, would let the user act
instead of discovering the problem mid-task.

The natural framework for anticipating a transition is **early-warning signals**
from dynamical systems theory — rising variance and rising autocorrelation as a
system's recovery from perturbation slows near a tipping point (Scheffer et al.,
2009; Dakos et al., 2008), with demonstrations in human neural data (Maturana et
al., 2020; Meisel et al., 2015). The framework is genuinely contested: Wilkat et
al. (2019) found no such evidence prior to epileptic seizures, Helmich et al.
(2024) argue the clinical support is thin, and van der Bolt et al. (2021) show
the required record length scales with how slowly the system responds — a
result that applies directly here.

**A pilot study conducted for this project tested that framework directly**, on
the Pun et al. dataset, under a design frozen in advance. It returned a negative
result, and the reasons are what shaped the present plan: no observable in the
data had a measurable recovery rate, so the autocorrelation half of the theory
could not be tested at all; the variance indicator turned out to be 71% mean
firing rate, which itself fell 56.5% across the record; and, decisively, the
indicator rose *faster during periods of healthy 93–100% performance* than it did
overall. An indicator that is not silent when the system is healthy is not a
detector. (Full record: `reports/PHASE1_2_REPORT.md`.)

That pilot also exposed a deeper problem, which is the reason this project
includes an original experiment. **In observational data, no one knows when
deterioration actually began.** The onset is defined by the analyst after the
fact, so any claim about how *early* a warning arrived is partly an artefact of
that definition, and the false-alarm rate cannot be estimated at all. Lead time
and false-alarm rate — the only two numbers that determine whether a warning
system is worth deploying — become measurable only in a system where the
experimenter controls, and logs in advance, when degradation starts.

This project therefore builds that system, and builds the monitor to be tested in
it. The societal case is direct: iBCIs are moving from research demonstrations
toward clinical use, and a device whose reliability cannot be monitored is a
device whose users cannot trust it. Knowing *when* to recalibrate — and being
told *why* — is a prerequisite for a neural interface someone can depend on
daily.

## B. Engineering Goal, Hypotheses, and Expected Outcomes

*(This is an engineering project with testable hypotheses; both headings apply.
The form permits keeping only applicable headings.)*

**Engineering Goal.** Design, build, and validate `decoder-guard`: a real-time
monitor that reads the same neural feature stream a BCI decoder reads and outputs
an interpretable decoder-health state — a calibrated risk score, a discrete
warning level, and an attribution naming which failure mode is responsible —
early enough and reliably enough to drive a recalibration decision.

**Hypotheses.**

- **H1 (lead time).** For degradations of known, pre-logged onset,
  `decoder-guard` reaches `WARN` before closed-loop task performance crosses its
  degradation threshold, with median lead time > 0 at a false-alarm rate ≤ 1 per
  10 hours of matched healthy operation.
- **H2 (specificity).** Attribution accuracy across failure modes exceeds
  chance, and genuine task changes are labelled `TASK-CHANGE` rather than as
  failures.
- **H3 (transfer).** The same monitor, structurally unmodified, passes the
  silence gate on the public intracortical dataset — where the pilot's indicator
  did not.
- **H4 (impact).** A recalibration policy driven by `WARN` achieves performance
  non-inferior to fixed-schedule recalibration with significantly fewer
  recalibrations.

**How this follows from the rationale.** H1 is the question Pun et al. did not
ask (anticipation rather than nowcast). H2 exists because the pilot found an
indicator that gave nearly identical values during a cursor task and during free
web browsing — a monitor that cannot separate "something broke" from "the user is
doing something else" will not survive real use. H3 is the pilot's failure turned
into a pass/fail criterion. H4 is the only hypothesis that measures benefit
rather than detection.

**Expected outcomes.** Either the gates are passed, giving a validated monitor
with quantified lead time and false-alarm rate; or they are not, giving a
quantified account of why a class of instability measures fails on neural
interfaces, together with the benchmark that establishes it. **The design is
deliberately constructed so that both outcomes are reportable**, and the pilot
demonstrates this is not a rhetorical device — a frozen design there produced a
negative result that was reported as such.

**Falsification, stated in advance.** H1 fails if median lead time ≤ 0 or the
false-alarm constraint is unmeetable at any operating point. H3 fails if the
monitor trends during any healthy baseline segment.

## C. Research Methods / Project Summary

### Materials and Equipment

*Final list depends on the signal-source decision — `[[OPEN — see
PROJECT_DEFINITION §11]]`. Both configurations are listed; delete the unused one
before submission.*

**Computing (all configurations)**
- Personal computer, Python 3.11+ with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, scikit-learn,
  Matplotlib, h5py
- Git / GitHub for version control and preregistration
- Public dataset: Pun et al. (2024), Dryad `doi:10.5061/dryad.n2z34tn5s`
  (~9 GB; already downloaded with SHA-256 verification)

**Configuration 1 — hardware-in-the-loop replay rig** *(no human participants)*
- Microcontroller development board with multichannel DAC (e.g. Teensy 4.1 or
  equivalent), for replaying recorded activity as analog signals
- Commercial multichannel biopotential amplifier / ADC board, battery-powered
- Analog switching network for programmable channel dropout and attenuation
- Breadboard, shielded cabling, passive components
- Bench multimeter

**Configuration 2 — surface EMG closed-loop control** *(human participants →
Form 4)*
- **Commercially manufactured, battery-powered, electrically isolated** surface
  EMG amplifier with ≥4 channels (no self-built circuitry connected to a person —
  see Risk and Safety)
- Disposable pre-gelled Ag/AgCl surface electrodes, single-use per participant
- Skin-prep wipes, medical tape, non-latex
- Monitor and standard input devices for the cursor task

*No chemicals with an NFPA rating of 3 or 4, or a GHS rating of 1, 2, or 3, are
used. No biological agents. No vertebrate animals.*

### Procedures

*Phase 1–2 procedures are already executed and documented in detail as 40
numbered steps in `research/procedures.md`; they are summarised here as items
1–4. Items 5 onward are the work this plan proposes.*

1. **Literature review** across three areas — iBCI signal non-stationarity,
   early-warning-signal theory and its critics, and human–decoder co-adaptation —
   with each claim classified as established, inference, or speculation.
2. **Dataset acquisition and characterisation.** Programmatic download with
   checksum verification; complete inventory of files, variables, dtypes, and
   unit of observation; documentation separating verified from interpreted claims
   (`DATASET_README.md`, `reports/DATASET_EXPLORATION.md`).
3. **Pipeline validation by reproduction.** Reproduce the published instability
   result from the source paper before attempting anything new
   (achieved: r = 0.985 vs the published 0.985).
4. **Preregistered pilot analysis.** Compare six candidate definitions of
   "deterioration" against fixed criteria; freeze one, together with all
   analysis choices, in a machine-readable record with a git commit hash and file
   checksums, *before* computing any indicator; run it once; report the result.
   (Result: negative — see Rationale.)
5. **Specify the monitor.** Define the feature abstraction (channels × binned
   activity), the one-class healthy reference model, the risk score and its
   decomposition into named contributions, the state machine with hysteresis and
   dwell times, and the attribution classifier over failure modes.
6. **Build the degradation injector.** Implement four failure modes — rate loss,
   channel dropout, geometry rotation, gain drift — each parameterised by onset
   time, rate, and endpoint severity. Onset times are drawn randomly and
   **written to a log file before the session runs**.
7. **Build the testbed.** Assemble the signal chain, feature extraction, decoder,
   and cursor task; verify closed-loop latency and that the injector's effects
   are measurable at the feature level.
8. **Collect the controlled corpus.** Run sessions across the full factorial of
   failure mode × rate × severity, including `NONE` control sessions of matched
   duration and `TASK-CHANGE` sessions in which the task changes but nothing
   degrades. Counterbalance mode order.
9. **Fit the monitor on healthy data only.** The reference model sees no
   degradation labels at any point. Choose the operating point on a validation
   split.
10. **Freeze the design.** Record all hyperparameters, thresholds, and the
    analysis plan using the same preregistration mechanism as step 4, before the
    test data are opened.
11. **Evaluate once on held-out data**, computing lead time, false-alarm rate,
    attribution confusion matrix, and calibration.
12. **Run the five gates** in reporting order, silence gate first.
13. **Transfer test.** Run the unmodified monitor on the public intracortical
    dataset (T11 and T5) and apply the same gates.
14. **Impact demonstration.** Compare three recalibration policies —
    monitor-triggered, fixed-schedule, never — on task performance and
    recalibration count.
15. **Report**, including any gate that fails and any hypothesis that is
    rejected.

### Risk and Safety

**Computational work:** no physical risk.

**Configuration 1 (replay rig):** low-voltage (≤5 V), battery- or USB-powered
bench electronics, not connected to any person and not connected to mains-powered
equipment while in contact with anything. Standard practice: no exposed mains
voltage, soldering with ventilation and eye protection under adult supervision,
components disposed of as electronic waste rather than household refuse.

**Configuration 2 (surface EMG on human participants):** this is the reason the
Human Participants section is completed. The controlling safety rule is that
**only a commercially manufactured, battery-powered, electrically isolated
biopotential amplifier is connected to a participant** — no student-built
circuitry, and no mains-powered device in the signal path to the skin. Electrodes
are single-use, pre-gelled, disposed of after each participant. Skin irritation is
the realistic risk and is minimised by non-latex adhesives, limiting wear time,
and stopping immediately on any report of discomfort.

**Note on Form 3.** Attaching an electronic device to a human participant may
cause the Rules Wizard to require Form 3 (Hazardous Activities and Devices) in
addition to Form 4. `[[RESEARCHER]]` — run the Rules Wizard after the signal
source is chosen and confirm with the Adult Sponsor and SRC; **do not assume this
project is Form 4 only.**

**Environmental impact:** negligible; electronic components and used electrodes
disposed of per local guidance.

### Data Analysis

**Primary analysis.** Lead time is computed per degradation episode as the signed
interval between the monitor's first `WARN` and the performance-threshold
crossing, where onset and threshold rule are both fixed before data collection.
The primary statistic is the **median lead time at a fixed false-alarm rate**,
with confidence intervals by bootstrap over episodes. Median rather than mean
because the distribution is expected to be skewed and occasionally censored (no
warning issued).

**Why not AUC.** A single discrimination number hides the tradeoff that actually
determines usefulness. Lead time at a constrained false-alarm rate states the
operating point explicitly.

**The five gates**, applied in this order and reported whatever the outcome:

1. **Silence gate.** No significant trend in the risk score during healthy
   operation (α = 0.05), tested on every healthy segment. This is checked
   *first*; a monitor that fails it is not interpreted further.
2. **Rate invariance.** Demonstrated, not asserted, on baseline data.
3. **Trivial comparator.** Must outperform mean signal amplitude alone.
4. **Elapsed-time control.** Results must survive regressing out time.
5. **De-trending.** Trend tests are run on de-trended series, an omission in the
   pilot's preregistration that the pilot itself identified.

**Statistical procedures.** Kendall's τ for monotonic trend (rank-based,
robust to the non-normal distributions observed in the pilot); AR(1)-matched
surrogate and permutation nulls rather than parametric p-values, following the
evaluation template of Wilkat et al. (2019); two-sided tests throughout, since
an indicator moving in the *opposite* direction is evidence against the
mechanism, not evidence for it; Benjamini–Hochberg correction across the gate
family; bootstrap confidence intervals over episodes and sessions.

**Leakage and overfitting controls.** One-class fitting on healthy data only;
splits by session and participant, never by window within a session; operating
point frozen before the test set is opened; test set evaluated exactly once;
preregistration recorded with a git commit hash and file checksums so that the
ordering of decisions is verifiable by a third party rather than asserted.

**Power.** A power analysis is run before data collection to set the number of
episodes per condition, using the effect sizes observed in the pilot's synthetic
controls. The pilot established that detection power depends strongly on record
length (power rose from 0.42 at 8,000 samples to 1.00 at 40,000), so episode
duration is set by that analysis rather than by convenience.

### Artificial Intelligence (AI)

*`[[RESEARCHER]]` — verify this against the 2026-27 rules and with your SRC
before submission; the AI provisions change year to year and the form lists
inappropriate AI use as grounds for disqualification.*

AI is used in this project in two distinct roles, which are disclosed separately
because they carry different obligations.

**1. AI as a research assistant (not part of the project's system).** A large
language model assistant (Claude, Anthropic) was and is used for: writing and
debugging Python analysis code; explaining statistical methods and dataset
structure; drafting and organising documentation; and acting as a critic of the
research design. All of this work is logged. Specifically, the repository
contains a dated research log recording what was done, why, and what went wrong;
every analysis script is version-controlled and re-runnable; and the study design
was frozen in a machine-readable record before the confirmatory analysis was run.

The scientific decisions — the research question, the choice of dataset, the
definition of deterioration, the decision to report a negative result, and the
choice of project direction — are the student's, made from options and evidence
presented for evaluation. The student can explain and defend every analysis in
the repository, and the reproduction of a published result (r = 0.985) is
included specifically as evidence that the pipeline was understood well enough
to be checked against ground truth.

**2. Machine learning inside the project's system.** `decoder-guard` uses
statistical and machine-learning methods as engineered components: a one-class
model of the healthy feature distribution, and a classifier for failure-mode
attribution. These are the student's implementations, trained on the student's
data, and are part of the artefact being evaluated rather than a tool used to
produce it. Model choice favours interpretable methods because interpretability
is a stated project requirement, not an afterthought.

No AI system generated data, results, or figures presented as experimental
findings. No AI-generated text is presented as the student's own scientific
conclusion without the student's own verification of the underlying analysis.

## Human Participants Research

**Applicable only under Configuration 2 (EMG).** If the project runs on the

The form requires six initialled acknowledgements here, a sample ISEF Human
Informed Consent Form attached in final form, and SRC approval **before**
experimentation begins. The tables below are drafted to the extent they can be;
every `[[RESEARCHER]]` field is one only the researcher can answer.

**My project involves:** Health/Medicine (physical) — *the project records a
physiological signal from participants.* Not survey, not food/drink, not media,
not social media. Whether it counts as exercise/physical exertion depends on the
task: sustained muscle contraction for cursor control is plausibly beyond a
participant's normal daily activity, and `[[RESEARCHER]]` should raise this
explicitly with the SRC rather than checking "no" by default.

|---|---|

| **Age range** | Proposed: 18+ only, to avoid the additional minor-participant requirements `[[RESEARCHER]]` |
| **Gender / racial-ethnic composition** | `[[RESEARCHER]]` — describe the actual recruited sample |
| **Protected groups** | None, if 18+ and not recruited from a facility. Confirm. |
| **Recruitment — where** | `[[RESEARCHER]]` |
| **Recruitment — how asked** | Verbal or written invitation with the consent form provided in advance; participation voluntary, withdrawal at any time without consequence |
| **At a facility housing protected groups?** | Proposed: No. If a school is used, written approval is required. |
| **Methods overview** | Participants have 4+ pre-gelled surface electrodes applied to the forearm, then use muscle activity to move a cursor to targets on a screen in sessions of approximately `[[RESEARCHER]]` minutes. During some sessions the software degrades the signal it receives — this changes how the cursor responds; **it does not change anything about the electrodes or what the participant experiences physically.** Participants are told in advance that this will happen. |
| **Handouts** | No paper materials distributed |
| **Online activities** | No |
| **Food or drink** | No |
| **Music or movies** | No |
| **Risks / discomforts** | Mild skin irritation from adhesive electrodes; muscle fatigue from sustained contraction; time commitment; frustration when the cursor responds poorly during degraded blocks |
| **Minimising risks** | Non-latex adhesives; limited wear time; rest breaks scheduled between blocks; participants told the cursor will sometimes behave badly **and that this is the experiment, not their failure**; session stops immediately on request or on any report of discomfort |
| **Benefits** | No direct benefit to participants. Societal benefit: methods for monitoring the reliability of assistive neural interfaces used by people with paralysis |
| **Identifiable information collected** | Name and signature on the consent form only; no identifiers in the data files |
| **Confidential or anonymous** | Data are anonymous; consent forms are kept separately and cannot be linked to data files |
